E tolls - reviving a dead horse

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Etolls are back front and centre of Gautengs conversation. Will we or wont we have to pay? Carte Blanche gets on the road again

Unique Selling Point:
Provincial and National government are at odds over this massive politcal hot potato

Summary:
Proposal
Paul Tati, a Roodepoort attorney has lost track of how much money he owes for his e-tolls.
"I nicely file it into file 13" he says. "Why must I pay to go to work."

Tati's wife works near Megawatt Park and every day she uses the highway. He estimates that her usage alone has run up a bill of around R300 000. "I am not going to pay it!" He says emphatically. "Look, I go to work and at the end of the month tax comes off my salary. Then I go to the petrol station and I pay more tax. Then I buy groceries and I pay tax yet again. Why must I now pay more tax!" he asks.

Since 2013, almost 70% of Gauteng's three million highway users have refused to pay their e-toll bills, which has left SANRAL the road agency with a headache. They are facing downgrades, they cant raise money on the bond markets, and they are deeply in debt. So much so the new finance minister Tito Mboweni has just announced a R5 billion rand bailout in his MTBPS. Ironically all this could have been avoided if government had taken OUTA'S advice in 2013 and added 10cents to the fuel levy to pay off the roads. Had they done so, by now the entire debt will have been paid off. Instead the GFIP has become the ANC's Gauteng failure - and they are now sitting with a R67 billion rand debt.


Further information:
MIXED MESSAGES
In February last year Gauteng Premier David Makhura said the following about the despised E tolls. " We are mobilizing resources for public transport infrastructure in ways tht will ensure that we don't commit the same mistakes done with E- tolls. We cant build roads and only later inform citizens that they must pay…I must admit publicly as I did last year that all the efforts we have made through the Advisory Panel have not led to the resolution of concerns of Gauteng motorists regarding affordability. We have tried our best, the ultimate solution must come from National Government.

Then last week, Gauteng motorists were crushed, then defiant as minister TITO MBOWENI made it clear that nothing really had changed. We must pay our tolls and it soon became clear that SANRAL was back to its same old bullying tactics once again.

But Makura was having none of it and shortly after he proclaimed: "Let there be no confusion, they are not part of the future of this province. We will have to work out how to pay for the roads but not through the e-tolls."

On Friday OUTA will join Cosatu and the SACP in a march against E TOLLS. But if there is one issue that unites South Africans its e-tolls. Rodney Thorpe on the East Rand is a business man who runs Johannesburg timbers. His trucks ply the highways and he thinks he owes about a million rand by now. He has received a summons from SANRAL and he too refuses to pay. If they come after me I will rather liquidate my business he says, and it's clear he isn't joking. He has just handed over all the documents to OUTA and hopes that they will sort it out.



Rudie Heyneke has been busy. Recently he compiled a detailed report that has gone to the president and various cabinet ministers. In it he sets out the numbers in meticulous detail, and its clear something has gone very wrong. How, for example can roads that we were told in 2011 would cost R16 billion rand - and all in phase one and two would cost R20 billion. Now phase two has been abandoned and Gauteng motorists are expected to cough up R67 billion. Yes R67 billion!

Carte Blanche will navigate through the confusion, once again put SANRAL on the spot, and bring you the staggering numbers incurred on your behalf, show you how R3.8 billion rand has gone offshore, and illustrate how your non -compliance with the new AARTO bill could turn you into a motoring criminal.

Press Release:


E-Tolls: on the Road Again
During Finance Minister Tito Mboweni’s medium-term budget speech, he made it clear that motorists would have no choice but to pay their e-toll accounts. Gauteng however remains defiant and Premier Makhura hit back, saying e-tolls are not part of the future of this province. Meanwhile, summonses for millions of rands are landing on desks across the province. So what happens now? Carte Blanche meets the man who has put up his hand to be the first test case.
Producer: Joy Summers
Presenter: Derek Watts
Research: Siniketiwe Hlanze
Watch the trailer


Script:


Final script E tolls 2018 TX Sunday 11th November 2018 FINAL FOR GRAPHICS

Commentary one
Road agency SANRAL has bullied, begged, and bargained with Gauteng motorists to pay for the upgrade of 186 kilometers of freeway. For five long years they have refused. Blocking highways

Hoot!

Bringing cities to a standstill

Struggle song!

And burning wheelchairs

Panzi E tolls! Panzi!

Opposition to e tolls unites South Africans, and divides politicians, as six cabinet ministers have tried unsuccessfully to solve Gauteng’s open road tolling fiasco

Wayne
It was always going to fail because it never had the support of the people

Commentary Two
Wayne Duvenage, founder of Outa has always maintained etolls were opaque, unfair, and unaffordable. They have been to court and won, then later lost, but motorists still heeded their call not to pay. In short, they became SANRAL’S nightmare

Derek
What has been the effect on SANRAL of the whole Gauteng project?
Vusi Mona
Look it’s taken its toll on us, excuse the pun! laughs
Derek
You have used that before?
They laugh

Commentary three
Spokesperson Vusi Mona is on the front lines at SANRAL.
Vusi
And we have had to take a step back and say how do we regain the confidence of the public

Commentary four
In 2014 they wanted to turn motorists into criminals. Now SANRAL is trying a softer approach.



Vusi
Are we going to turn people into criminals? I think no, so we are opting to go the civil route because what we are interested in is, getting the money

Commentary five
Money they desperately need to pay their debts. Every month they have a shortfall of around R135 million

Derek
What is the debt owed by e tolls?
Vusi
I think its sitting at about R9 or ten billion.

Up sound clapping

Commentary six
So, who’s going to pay the bills? We are! said the new finance minister Tito Mboweni in his medium- term budget speech

Tito Mboweni
If we want the road network to work, we must therefore pay our tolls

Commentary seven
Not so fast, retorted Gauteng Premier David Makhura, who understands what millions of summonses across Gauteng could mean for the ANC at the next elections

Premier David Makhura
I don’t want to respond to a government minister! I am here to ensure that the conference resolution of the ANC is implemented. E tolls are not part of the future of this province!

Commentary eight
The premier made this statement at a march last Friday organized by Cosatu. But it was an odd march of the ANC marching against a policy signed into law by …well the ANC

Siniketiwe
Mr. Mayor the ANC Is marching to the ANC to tell the ANC that ….
Mayor Masina
No, no, no the ANC in Gauteng is marching to the ANC led government in SA – we want to send a message to the president that the cost of living is too high

Up sound
Viva comrade DG! Viva

Commentary nine
In a memorandum to Minister Jeff Radebe, they demanded the unconditional scrapping of e tolls, alternative funding options, and that the President institute a forensic investigation into the real cost of the freeways. But Sanral want their money and they have business in their sights

Vusi
The bulk of that debt- 80% of it is sitting with business- which is unfortunate

LINK
SANRAL says the biggest debt owed to them is from the corporate sector, businesses like this one say that if they have to pay all their outstanding e- tolls they would rather close down

Commentary ten
This palette business just off the highway, has been around for almost 80 years. Its owner, Rodney Thorpe runs a tight ship with slim profit margins around 8 %. E tolls he says, would have pushed the business over the edge.

Up sound staple gun

This year he got a summons from Sanral

Derek
Hefty document Rodney, how do you feel when something like this, lands on your doorstep?
Rodney
From my perspective I thought this is not real, this is got to be a dream. This is not happening to us.

Commentary eleven
With a staff of about 400, the summons for over half a million rand has been giving Rodney sleepless nights

Rodney
We are a little bit anxious, if it did go the full hog and we had to go to court and lose, we would probably have to shut up shop and pay off 400 people

Derek Link
The costs of the roads seems to have been a moving target, starting out as a R14 billion project – the total cost over 24 years is said to have spiraled to R90 billion

Commentary twelve
But as Outa’s Rudie Heyneke points out, if government had listened to them five years ago, the debts would already have been paid

Derek
Outa says from the start put 10 cents on the fuel levy?


Rudie
That is right and if that had been done from the start the debts would have been paid off by now

Commentary thirteen
But how could roads budgeted at R14 billion escalate to R89 billion rand? Well that figure which includes interest and the original debt was submitted by the former CEO Nazir Ali to the Constitutional court in 2012. If that is so, Sanral would need ten million rand per day for 24 years says OUTA

Rudie
We know now for the whole financial year they only collected R725 million and if you do the calculations you can see that we will never get to R10 million per day.

LINK
It’s not just the cost of the roads, the enormous cost of collecting toll fees has also enraged Gauteng Motorists

Commentary fourteen
That is another R3.8 billion rand paid to the collection companies between 2009 and 2017 says this report published by OUTA.

Rudie
They are just collecting to pay the collectors.

Commentary fifteen
ETC the collection company, confirmed they were paid R3.8 billion for the development and implementation of a tolling system, which includes collecting the tolls.

Derek link
For a few years Gauteng motorists and businesses ignored e tolls but as hefty summonses have been landing on Gauteng desks, the motorists have become rather jittery

Commentary sixteen
Verna Naidoo has a small fleet of trucks. Initially he was going to pay his etolls, but he wanted the controversy to be ironed out first

Verna
I am a law -abiding citizen, and I thought it was the right thing to do

Commentary seventeen
But as the economy contracted, his business did too, so, he never paid. Then he received a summons from Sanral for over a million rand.

Derek
Did you get a huge shock when you got the summons in 2016?
Verna
I did get a huge shock because it’s a helluva lot of money and there is no way I can afford to pay that

Commentary eighteen
He turned to OUTA for help and will now be one of the first test cases

Derek
What if you lose case and have to pay by then half a million or more
Verna
I can assure you that I will seriously consider closing my business down. I am not doing this because I am defiant. I am doing this because it’s a system that is destroying us.

Derek
We have spoken to business men who say they would rather close shop because they can’t afford
Vusi
I get a sense they may be exaggerating but I say this guardedly
Derek
One case study says he owes about a million rand
Vusi
And how much is he making, because it’s very easy to say you owe a million but how much is coming into the business

Commentary nineteen
So far about 11 000 summonses have been issued but around 2 million motorists don’t pay etolls.

Vusi
Even after we issue summons, we say to motorists if you are prepared to enter into an arrangement with us to say this is what I can afford to pay, let’s sit down.

Commentary twenty
OUTA recommends that if you receive a summons don’t ignore it.

Rudie
If you do not defend the matter SANRAL can take a default judgement after a certain period of time, if you defend the matter then SANRAL can give us a declaration of their claim so we can see what it is all about.

Commentary Twenty- one
But if SANRAL want to collect all their arrears they will have to summons 2 million motorists at an average cost of around R1600 per summons

Derek
Vusi would you concede that in the present form ETOLLS cannot not work?
Vusi
If South Africans can appreciate why they have to pay for this infrastructure it will work?
Derek
I don’t think you have a hope of convincing them, that is my view?
Vusi
Well Derek there was a time when the graph was going upward
Derek
Really?
Vusi
Oh yes,
Derek
With more than 70% of motorists not paying?
Vusi
Things started changing when the Gauteng government put doubt in the minds of motorists. That was the turning point
Derek
So, what is going to change now, because the Premier is still against it?
Vusi
When it comes to the premier I would rather he engages with the minister. I am a civil servant

Commentary twenty- two
But this week the transport minister Blade Nzimande told parliament that government is not scrapping e-tolls and those who derive economic benefit from using the roads should pay for them. ETC, the TOLL collection company told us on Friday they are optimistic a solution would be forthcoming in the next few months

THE END 10 mins 03

PROMO ONE 10 seconds
E tolls have been in the news again. The politicians are divided as 2 million Gauteng motorists refuse to pay their e tolls. We go back to Sanral for answers.

PROMO TWO 15 seconds
We speak to Gauteng businesses who would rather shut shop than pay their outstanding toll fees.
Verna
I am not doing this because I am defiant. I am doing this because the system is killing us

PROMO THREE 15 seconds
Sanral is in debt as Gauteng motorists refuse to pay etolls. Now Sanral has issued 11 000 summonses to pay -up

Rodney
From my perspective I thought hey this is not real, this has to be a dream, this is not happening to us.

PROMO FOUR 30 seconds
Sanral still believe they can convince Gauteng motorists to pay their etolls
Derek
Vusi would you concede that in the present form ETOLLS will not work?
Vusi
If South Africans can appreciate why they have to pay for this infrastructure it will work?
Derek
I don’t think you have a hope of convincing them, that is my view?
Vusi
Well Derek there was a time when the graph was going upward. Things started changing when the Gauteng government started putting doubt in the minds of Gauteng motorists

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Etolls are back front and centre of Gautengs conversation. Will we or wont we have to pay? Carte Blanche gets on the road again
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Provincial and National government are at odds over this massive politcal hot potato
metadata.Summary: Proposal Paul Tati, a Roodepoort attorney has lost track of how much money he owes for his e-tolls. "I nicely file it into file 13" he says. "Why must I pay to go to work." Tati's wife works near Megawatt Park and every day she uses the highway. He estimates that her usage alone has run up a bill of around R300 000. "I am not going to pay it!" He says emphatically. "Look, I go to work and at the end of the month tax comes off my salary. Then I go to the petrol station and I pay more tax. Then I buy groceries and I pay tax yet again. Why must I now pay more tax!" he asks. Since 2013, almost 70% of Gauteng's three million highway users have refused to pay their e-toll bills, which has left SANRAL the road agency with a headache. They are facing downgrades, they cant raise money on the bond markets, and they are deeply in debt. So much so the new finance minister Tito Mboweni has just announced a R5 billion rand bailout in his MTBPS. Ironically all this could have been avoided if government had taken OUTA'S advice in 2013 and added 10cents to the fuel levy to pay off the roads. Had they done so, by now the entire debt will have been paid off. Instead the GFIP has become the ANC's Gauteng failure - and they are now sitting with a R67 billion rand debt.
metadata.Further information: MIXED MESSAGES In February last year Gauteng Premier David Makhura said the following about the despised E tolls. " We are mobilizing resources for public transport infrastructure in ways tht will ensure that we don't commit the same mistakes done with E- tolls. We cant build roads and only later inform citizens that they must pay…I must admit publicly as I did last year that all the efforts we have made through the Advisory Panel have not led to the resolution of concerns of Gauteng motorists regarding affordability. We have tried our best, the ultimate solution must come from National Government. Then last week, Gauteng motorists were crushed, then defiant as minister TITO MBOWENI made it clear that nothing really had changed. We must pay our tolls and it soon became clear that SANRAL was back to its same old bullying tactics once again. But Makura was having none of it and shortly after he proclaimed: "Let there be no confusion, they are not part of the future of this province. We will have to work out how to pay for the roads but not through the e-tolls." On Friday OUTA will join Cosatu and the SACP in a march against E TOLLS. But if there is one issue that unites South Africans its e-tolls. Rodney Thorpe on the East Rand is a business man who runs Johannesburg timbers. His trucks ply the highways and he thinks he owes about a million rand by now. He has received a summons from SANRAL and he too refuses to pay. If they come after me I will rather liquidate my business he says, and it's clear he isn't joking. He has just handed over all the documents to OUTA and hopes that they will sort it out. Rudie Heyneke has been busy. Recently he compiled a detailed report that has gone to the president and various cabinet ministers. In it he sets out the numbers in meticulous detail, and its clear something has gone very wrong. How, for example can roads that we were told in 2011 would cost R16 billion rand - and all in phase one and two would cost R20 billion. Now phase two has been abandoned and Gauteng motorists are expected to cough up R67 billion. Yes R67 billion! Carte Blanche will navigate through the confusion, once again put SANRAL on the spot, and bring you the staggering numbers incurred on your behalf, show you how R3.8 billion rand has gone offshore, and illustrate how your non -compliance with the new AARTO bill could turn you into a motoring criminal.
